queries.query_text: What are the six principles of lawful processing under GDPR Article 5?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs rarely get this wrong — the six principles (lawfulness/fairness/transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity/confidentiality) are well-documented and frequently cited in training data

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may check whether the LLM correctly lists all six principles without adding fabricated ones or omitting storage limitation

queries.notes: Baseline query — validates that the MAD pipeline does not over-challenge correct, well-established regulatory content

queries.query_text: What are the five core functions of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs sometimes omit the sixth function 'Govern' added in CSF 2.0 and only list the original five (Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), but the five original functions are always correct

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may challenge whether the LLM mentions Govern as the new sixth function in CSF 2.0 versus the original five in CSF 1.1

queries.notes: Baseline for NIST knowledge — if Agent A flags this as unsupported, calibration is broken

queries.query_text: What is the definition of a covered entity under HIPAA?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs correctly identify the three categories (health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, healthcare providers who transmit electronically) but sometimes incorrectly include business associates as covered entities rather than a separate category

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may check whether the LLM correctly distinguishes covered entities from business associates

queries.notes: Fundamental HIPAA definition — validates that well-established concepts pass through without false challenges

queries.query_text: What is the legal basis for processing personal data under GDPR Article 6?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs consistently list the six lawful bases correctly (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests) — this is one of the most frequently cited GDPR provisions

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B unlikely to find strong challenge material; may verify completeness of all six bases

queries.notes: Core GDPR provision — establishes that the pipeline correctly handles unambiguous regulatory content

queries.query_text: What are the main control domains defined in ISO 27001:2022 Annex A?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs sometimes cite the old 14-domain structure from ISO 27001:2013 instead of the 2022 reorganisation into 4 themes (Organisational, People, Physical, Technological) with 93 controls

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may challenge if the LLM describes the 2013 structure instead of the 2022 revision

queries.notes: Tests whether the RAG retrieves the 2022 version — the 2013-to-2022 structural change is a known LLM confusion point

queries.query_text: What rights does the CCPA grant to California consumers regarding their personal information?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs generally list the core rights (know, delete, opt-out of sale, non-discrimination) correctly but may miss CPRA additions like right to correct and right to limit use of sensitive personal information

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may verify whether CPRA amendments are reflected in the response

queries.notes: Baseline for US state privacy law — well-established consumer rights that should pass validation

queries.query_text: What is the purpose of the NIST Secure Software Development Framework (SSDF)?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs occasionally confuse SSDF with the general NIST CSF or with NIST SP 800-53 controls, but the high-level purpose statement is usually correct

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may check whether the LLM correctly identifies SSDF as focused on software development practices rather than general cybersecurity

queries.notes: Validates NIST SSDF RAG retrieval — the purpose is well-defined and should produce a clean SUPPORTED verdict

queries.query_text: What are the key data subject rights guaranteed under GDPR Chapter III?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs reliably list the main rights (access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection) but sometimes omit the right not to be subject to automated decision-making (Art 22)

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may check completeness — whether Art 22 automated decision-making is included

queries.notes: Well-established GDPR content that should produce high-confidence SUPPORTED verdicts

queries.query_text: What categories of AI systems are classified as prohibited under the EU AI Act?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs generally list social scoring, real-time biometric identification, and manipulative AI correctly, but may miss newer additions like emotion recognition in workplaces/schools or untargeted scraping for facial recognition databases

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may verify the LLM includes the full list of prohibited practices from Article 5 rather than just the commonly cited ones

queries.notes: Tests EU AI Act knowledge — the prohibited practices list is well-publicised but the full list is longer than most LLMs reproduce

queries.query_text: What does the Singapore PDPA require organisations to do before collecting personal data?
queries.hallucination_risk: high — also IDK risk if RAG chunks are sparse for this regulation
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs usually correctly identify the consent and notification obligations but may incorrectly state that consent must be written when the PDPA accepts deemed consent in certain circumstances

expected_mad_outcome.likely_verdict: NOT_SUPPORTED or IDK — depends on RAG chunk coverage for this regulation
expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B may check whether deemed consent provisions are accurately described

queries.notes: Ensures non-EU/non-US regulation coverage in baseline — tests Singapore PDPA RAG retrieval

queries.query_text: What are the maximum fine amounts for GDPR violations under Article 83, and what types of violations fall under each tier?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently confuse the two tiers: Art 83(4) is up to EUR 10M or 2% of global turnover for controller/processor obligation violations, Art 83(5) is up to EUR 20M or 4% of global turnover for data subject rights and lawful basis violations. LLMs commonly state 4% as the only maximum or apply it to the wrong violation category

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge specific fine amounts and which violations map to which tier — LLMs almost always get the tier mapping wrong

queries.notes: High-value stress test — the two-tier fine structure is the most commonly hallucinated GDPR detail

queries.query_text: What is the exact timeframe for breach notification under GDPR Article 33, and who must be notified?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs correctly state 72 hours for supervisory authority notification but frequently hallucinate a specific timeframe for data subject notification under Art 34 — Art 34 says 'without undue delay' with no specific hour/day deadline. LLMs often fabricate '72 hours for data subjects too' or '30 days for data subjects'

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any specific timeframe cited for Art 34 data subject notification — the regulation deliberately avoids specifying one

queries.notes: Classic hallucination trap — LLMs impose false precision on Art 34's deliberately vague language

queries.query_text: What specific encryption standards does GDPR Article 32 require organisations to implement?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently hallucinate that GDPR mandates AES-256, TLS 1.2, or other specific encryption standards. Art 32 says 'appropriate technical and organisational measures' and lists encryption as one example but never specifies any standard. This is the exact hallucination the synthetic dataset was built around

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will cite the actual Art 32 text showing no encryption standard is named — this should be a strong, evidence-based challenge

queries.notes: Flagship hallucination test — mirrors the GDPR AES-256 example used in the synthetic training data and report

queries.query_text: What are the four penalty tiers under the HITECH Act for HIPAA violations, and what are the specific dollar amounts for each tier?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often cite outdated pre-2019 penalty amounts. The 2019 HHS inflation adjustment changed the tiers. LLMs also frequently confuse per-violation minimums with annual caps, or hallucinate specific amounts like $50,000 for Tier 2 when the actual amount differs

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge specific dollar amounts against the RAG source — exact figures are frequently hallucinated

queries.notes: Tests whether Agent A can detect its own overconfidence when citing specific penalty amounts from memory vs evidence

queries.query_text: What is the maximum response time a business must meet when a California consumer submits a CCPA data access request?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state 30 days (confusing with GDPR's one-month period) when the CCPA actually allows 45 calendar days with a possible 45-day extension. Some LLMs hallucinate a 10-business-day acknowledgment requirement that does not exist in the statute

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any 30-day timeframe and verify the 45+45 day structure from the CCPA text

queries.notes: Cross-regulation confusion test — LLMs conflate GDPR and CCPA response deadlines almost universally

queries.query_text: What conformity assessment requirements does the EU AI Act impose on high-risk AI systems before they can be placed on the market?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently hallucinate that all high-risk AI systems require third-party conformity assessment. In reality, most high-risk systems under Annex III can use self-assessment (internal control procedure) — only biometric identification systems and a few others require notified body involvement. LLMs also fabricate specific certification bodies or ISO standards as mandatory

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge the blanket third-party assessment claim with evidence that self-assessment is the default for most Annex III systems

queries.notes: Critical EU AI Act test — the self-assessment vs third-party distinction is one of the most misunderstood provisions

queries.query_text: What are the specific incident reporting timeframes required under the NIS2 Directive for essential entities?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state a single reporting deadline (24 or 72 hours) when NIS2 actually has a multi-stage reporting process: early warning within 24 hours, incident notification within 72 hours, and final report within one month. LLMs frequently omit the early warning stage or confuse the 24-hour and 72-hour deadlines

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any single-deadline answer with evidence of the three-stage reporting structure

queries.notes: NIS2 is recent enough that LLMs have poor coverage — the multi-stage reporting is almost never correctly reproduced

queries.query_text: What specific data retention periods does HIPAA mandate for medical records?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs commonly state that HIPAA requires 6 or 7 years of medical record retention. HIPAA actually does NOT mandate medical record retention periods — the 6-year requirement under 45 CFR 164.530(j) applies to HIPAA compliance documentation, not medical records. Medical record retention is governed by state law. This is one of the most persistent HIPAA misconceptions

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge the conflation of compliance documentation retention with medical record retention using the actual CFR text

queries.notes: Extremely common hallucination — the HIPAA-does-not-mandate-medical-record-retention fact surprises even compliance professionals

queries.query_text: What are the penalties for non-compliance with the EU Cyber Resilience Act for manufacturers of products with digital elements?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently hallucinate specific penalty amounts for the CRA or confuse them with GDPR fines. The CRA specifies up to EUR 15M or 2.5% of global annual turnover for the most serious violations, but LLMs often cite EUR 20M/4% (GDPR numbers) or fabricate entirely different amounts. Some LLMs claim the CRA has not been enacted yet when it was adopted in 2024

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge specific penalty figures against the CRA text — LLMs almost always import GDPR penalty structures here

queries.notes: Tests a very recent regulation — CRA penalty details are poorly represented in LLM training data

queries.query_text: Under the China PIPL, what are the conditions for cross-border transfer of personal information outside of China?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently describe PIPL cross-border transfer as identical to GDPR adequacy decisions. In reality, PIPL requires one of: passing a security assessment by the CAC (mandatory for critical information infrastructure operators and large-scale processors), obtaining personal information protection certification, entering standard contracts filed with the CAC, or meeting other conditions prescribed by law. LLMs omit the CAC security assessment requirement and the volume thresholds that trigger mandatory assessment

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any description that mirrors GDPR adequacy mechanisms without the China-specific CAC security assessment requirements

queries.notes: Critical test of non-Western regulation knowledge — LLMs default to GDPR-like descriptions for all privacy laws

queries.query_text: What specific vulnerability disclosure timeframes does the EU Cyber Resilience Act require from manufacturers?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often hallucinate specific hour or day deadlines for CRA vulnerability disclosure or confuse them with NIS2 incident reporting timelines. The CRA requires notification to ENISA within 24 hours of becoming aware of an actively exploited vulnerability, but LLMs frequently state different timeframes or confuse vulnerability disclosure with product incident reporting

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any fabricated timeframe with the actual CRA text on vulnerability notification to ENISA

queries.notes: Tests CRA-specific knowledge — LLMs frequently import NIS2 timelines into CRA answers

queries.query_text: What are the specific fines for violating the Digital Services Act's transparency obligations for very large online platforms?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently state GDPR-level fines or fabricate specific amounts. The DSA allows fines up to 6% of global annual turnover for VLOPs/VLOSEs, with periodic penalties up to 5% of average daily worldwide turnover. LLMs commonly state 4% (GDPR contamination) or fail to distinguish between VLOP fines and general provider fines

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge the 4% figure if cited and verify the 6% VLOP maximum from the DSA text

queries.notes: Tests DSA knowledge — the 6% figure is distinctive but LLMs default to 4% from GDPR familiarity

queries.query_text: What does the Japan APPI require regarding the appointment of a personal information protection officer?
queries.hallucination_risk: high — also IDK risk if RAG chunks are sparse for this regulation
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently state that the APPI requires all businesses to appoint a DPO equivalent, borrowing from GDPR Article 37 requirements. The APPI does not mandate a named officer role like the GDPR DPO — it requires 'necessary and appropriate supervision' of employees handling personal information but the specific organisational mechanism is left to the business

expected_mad_outcome.likely_verdict: NOT_SUPPORTED or IDK — depends on RAG chunk coverage for this regulation
expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any DPO mandate claim with the actual APPI supervisory obligation language

queries.notes: Tests whether LLMs project GDPR concepts onto non-EU privacy laws — a common hallucination pattern

queries.query_text: What is the minimum age for valid consent to data processing under GDPR, and can member states modify this threshold?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state 16 as a fixed EU-wide threshold. Art 8 sets 16 as the default but explicitly allows member states to lower it to as low as 13. LLMs frequently omit the member state derogation or incorrectly state the floor as 14 or 15 instead of 13. Some hallucinate that the UK set it at 12

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge if the member state derogation is omitted or if the minimum floor is stated incorrectly

queries.notes: Tests nuanced GDPR knowledge — the 16/13 default-with-derogation structure is frequently oversimplified

queries.query_text: What specific requirements does the Saudi PDPL impose for processing sensitive personal data?
queries.hallucination_risk: high — also IDK risk if RAG chunks are sparse for this regulation
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs typically describe GDPR Article 9 requirements and attribute them to the Saudi PDPL. The Saudi PDPL has its own definition of sensitive data and processing conditions that differ from GDPR — for example, it requires explicit consent and regulatory approval for certain categories, and its definition of sensitive data includes data revealing ethnic origin differently from GDPR's racial/ethnic distinction

expected_mad_outcome.likely_verdict: NOT_SUPPORTED or IDK — depends on RAG chunk coverage for this regulation
expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge GDPR-derived descriptions with the actual Saudi PDPL text from the RAG

queries.notes: Tests an underrepresented regulation — Saudi PDPL is in the RAG but rarely in LLM training data, so hallucination rates are very high

queries.query_text: Is encryption of electronic PHI at rest a required or addressable implementation specification under the HIPAA Security Rule?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state encryption is 'required' when it is actually an 'addressable' specification under 45 CFR 164.312(a)(2)(iv). Addressable does not mean optional — it means the entity must implement it OR document why an equivalent alternative measure is reasonable and appropriate. LLMs typically get the answer half-right by saying addressable but then incorrectly explain what addressable means

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge the nuance of 'addressable' — most LLM answers either say it's required (wrong) or say it's optional (also wrong)

queries.notes: Classic nuance test — the required/addressable/optional distinction in HIPAA is a three-way trap for LLMs

queries.query_text: Does GDPR Article 17 give data subjects an absolute right to erasure of their personal data?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often present the right to erasure as absolute when Art 17(3) lists significant exceptions: freedom of expression, legal obligations, public health, archival/research purposes, and legal claims. A simplified LLM answer omitting these exceptions is only partially correct

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any answer that presents erasure as unconditional without citing the Art 17(3) exceptions

queries.notes: Tests whether the pipeline correctly identifies oversimplification as PARTIAL rather than SUPPORTED or NOT_SUPPORTED

queries.query_text: Do the NIS2 Directive requirements apply equally to essential and important entities?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs typically describe NIS2 requirements as uniform when the Directive explicitly differentiates between essential and important entities in terms of supervisory regime (ex ante vs ex post), penalty levels, and specific obligations. Essential entities face stricter oversight including proactive audits, while important entities are subject to reactive supervision

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any answer that treats essential and important entities identically — the distinction is fundamental to NIS2's architecture

queries.notes: Tests whether the pipeline catches an answer that is correct on the general requirements but wrong on the differentiated treatment

queries.query_text: Does GDPR apply to small businesses with fewer than 250 employees?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often incorrectly state that GDPR exempts SMEs with fewer than 250 employees. Art 30(5) only exempts them from the records-of-processing-activities requirement, and even that exemption has exceptions (if processing is not occasional, involves special category data, or risks rights/freedoms). All other GDPR obligations apply regardless of size

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any blanket SME exemption claim — the 250-employee threshold only applies to one narrow obligation

queries.notes: Extremely common misconception — the SME 'exemption' is one of the most over-stated GDPR provisions

queries.query_text: Under HIPAA, can a covered entity share patient information with law enforcement without patient authorisation?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs either say yes unconditionally or no unconditionally. The correct answer is nuanced: 45 CFR 164.512(f) permits disclosure to law enforcement under six specific circumstances (court order, administrative subpoena, to identify a suspect/fugitive/witness, about a crime victim, about a decedent, to report a crime on premises) but not as a blanket exception. Each circumstance has specific conditions

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge either an unconditional yes or an unconditional no — the answer requires enumerating the specific permitted circumstances

queries.notes: Tests whether the pipeline handles a genuinely conditional answer — neither fully supported nor fully unsupported

queries.query_text: Are all AI systems that process biometric data classified as high-risk under the EU AI Act?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state that any biometric processing makes an AI system high-risk. The EU AI Act distinguishes between real-time remote biometric identification (prohibited in public spaces for law enforcement with narrow exceptions), post-remote biometric identification (high-risk), and other biometric systems that may not be high-risk. The classification depends on the specific use case, not merely the data type

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any blanket classification by citing the use-case-dependent distinction in the Act

queries.notes: Tests nuanced EU AI Act knowledge — the biometric classification is more complex than 'biometric = high-risk'

queries.query_text: Does the UK Online Safety Act 2023 apply to end-to-end encrypted messaging services?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often give a binary yes/no when the answer is deliberately ambiguous in the legislation. The Act technically applies to all user-to-user services including encrypted platforms, but the practical enforcement of content scanning obligations on E2E encrypted services remains contested. Section 122 allows Ofcom to require technology to identify CSAM content but includes a feasibility qualification

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any definitive yes or no — the correct answer must acknowledge the tension between legal scope and technical feasibility

queries.notes: Tests a genuinely ambiguous regulatory question where PARTIAL is the correct verdict

queries.query_text: Does GDPR consent need to be explicit for all types of personal data processing?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often conflate the consent requirements. Under Art 6, consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous — but not necessarily explicit. Explicit consent is only required for special category data under Art 9(2)(a) and for cross-border transfers under Art 49(1)(a). LLMs frequently state that all GDPR consent must be explicit, which is incorrect

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge the conflation of 'unambiguous' with 'explicit' — they are different GDPR consent standards

queries.notes: Tests a subtle but important GDPR distinction that most LLMs get wrong by oversimplifying

queries.query_text: Under the Council of Europe Convention 108, do signatory states have to implement the convention provisions identically?
queries.hallucination_risk: high — also IDK risk if RAG chunks are sparse for this regulation
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often describe Convention 108 as directly applicable like an EU regulation. Convention 108 is an international treaty that requires transposition into domestic law, giving signatory states flexibility in implementation. The modernised Convention 108+ (CETS 223) maintained this approach. LLMs frequently confuse treaty obligations with directly applicable law

expected_mad_outcome.likely_verdict: NOT_SUPPORTED or IDK — depends on RAG chunk coverage for this regulation
expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any description that implies direct applicability — the convention requires domestic implementation with national flexibility

queries.notes: Tests knowledge of an older, less-cited instrument — LLMs have thin coverage and tend to project EU regulation characteristics onto it

queries.query_text: Does the US Executive Order 14110 on AI create legally binding requirements for private companies developing AI systems?
queries.hallucination_risk: high — also IDK risk if RAG chunks are sparse for this regulation
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs frequently describe EO 14110 as creating binding obligations for all AI developers. Executive orders bind federal agencies, not private companies directly. EO 14110 directs agencies to develop standards and guidelines, requires reporting from companies developing dual-use foundation models above certain compute thresholds (via the Defense Production Act), but does not create a comprehensive private-sector regulatory framework like the EU AI Act

expected_mad_outcome.likely_verdict: NOT_SUPPORTED or IDK — depends on RAG chunk coverage for this regulation
expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any description that equates EO authority with statutory law — the legal mechanisms are fundamentally different

queries.notes: Tests understanding of US regulatory mechanisms — LLMs often conflate executive orders with legislation

queries.query_text: How do GDPR breach notification requirements under Article 33 interact with NIS2 incident reporting obligations for an organisation subject to both?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs typically describe only one regime or state they are identical. GDPR requires notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours for personal data breaches, while NIS2 has a three-stage process (24-hour early warning, 72-hour notification, one-month final report) for significant incidents. An organisation subject to both must comply with both timelines independently. LLMs often merge them into a single obligation or state that NIS2 compliance satisfies GDPR requirements

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any merged description — the two regimes have different triggers, timeframes, and reporting authorities

queries.notes: Critical cross-regulation test — dual-notification obligations are a real compliance challenge and LLMs consistently oversimplify them

queries.query_text: When an AI system processes personal data, how do the GDPR and EU AI Act requirements interact — does compliance with one satisfy the other?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state that GDPR compliance is sufficient for AI Act compliance or vice versa. The two regulations have overlapping but distinct requirements: GDPR governs the personal data processing, while the AI Act governs the AI system's risk classification, transparency, and conformity assessment. An AI system processing personal data must comply with both independently. The AI Act explicitly states it is without prejudice to GDPR. LLMs also often incorrectly state that the AI Act creates a new legal basis for data processing

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any claim that one regulation subsumes the other, citing the AI Act's 'without prejudice to GDPR' clause

queries.notes: Tests a real-world compliance question that enterprises face — the GDPR/AI Act intersection is one of the most misunderstood regulatory relationships

queries.query_text: How do HIPAA and CCPA interact for a California healthcare provider — does HIPAA pre-empt CCPA for patient data?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state that HIPAA completely pre-empts CCPA for healthcare providers. The CCPA explicitly exempts PHI governed by HIPAA, but the healthcare provider may hold non-PHI personal information (employee data, website visitor data, marketing data) that IS subject to CCPA. LLMs frequently state a blanket exemption when the exemption applies only to the specific data governed by HIPAA, not to the entity as a whole

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any blanket pre-emption claim — the exemption is data-specific, not entity-specific

queries.notes: Tests a practical US regulatory intersection — the HIPAA/CCPA data-level vs entity-level exemption is a common compliance error

queries.query_text: If an organisation holds ISO 27001:2022 certification, does that demonstrate compliance with GDPR Article 32 security requirements?
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state that ISO 27001 certification equals GDPR Art 32 compliance. While ISO 27001 covers many of the technical and organisational measures Art 32 requires, GDPR compliance is assessed contextually based on the specific data processing operations, risks, and state of the art. ISO 27001 is evidence of good security practices but is not a GDPR compliance certification. Art 42 discusses certification mechanisms but ISO 27001 is not one of them

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any equivalence claim — ISO 27001 is supportive evidence but not a GDPR compliance determination

queries.notes: Tests a common enterprise misconception — organisations frequently assume ISO certification satisfies GDPR requirements

queries.query_text: How do the OWASP AI security guidelines relate to the EU AI Act's requirements for high-risk AI system robustness?
queries.target_regulation: OWASP AI Security / EU AI Act 2024
queries.what_llm_typically_gets_wrong: LLMs often state that following OWASP AI guidelines satisfies EU AI Act robustness requirements. OWASP provides voluntary technical guidance on threats like prompt injection and model manipulation, while the EU AI Act imposes legal obligations around accuracy, robustness, and cybersecurity for high-risk systems. The AI Act does not reference OWASP specifically. LLMs conflate voluntary best practice frameworks with binding regulatory requirements

expected_mad_outcome.likely_agent_b_challenge: Agent B will challenge any claim that OWASP compliance satisfies AI Act obligations — the legal vs voluntary distinction is fundamental

queries.notes: Tests whether LLMs distinguish between voluntary guidance and binding law — a critical distinction for enterprise compliance

summary.purpose: MAD pipeline stress test — fact-checking and calibration evaluation
